On grammar, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan treat the particle 'an' as explanatory or verbal, while al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud link the clause to the word 'warner' in the preceding verse.

This verse reports Noah's call to his people: worship God, fear Him and obey him, so that God will forgive their sins and grant them a fixed term, since God's term, once it comes, cannot be delayed. The commentators agree on the general sense: faith opens the way to forgiveness and a longer life, and people should hasten to repent because they do not know what awaits them. They also agree that 'the term of God' refers either to the hour of death, the hour of punishment, or the Day of Resurrection.

Opinions differ on the particle 'min' in 'min dhunubikum'. Al-Tabari, followed by Ibn Kathir, takes it to mean 'an', so that God pardons them by overlooking their sins. Al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy regard it as an emphatic or specifying particle, or as an extra particle, while al-Razi and al-Nasafi take it as partitive, since Islam wipes out what came before conversion. Ibn Atiyya judges this last reading the clearest, and Mujahid, Ibn Jarir and the Jalalayn add that the rights of people are not included.

The 'term' also gives rise to differences. The Mu'tazilites, as reported by Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy, infer that each person has two terms; Ibn Atiyya replies that Noah did not know his people's fate and that the decree was already settled. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di understand that obedience may lengthen life and avert punishment. Ibn 'Ashur distinguishes the eternal decree, which does not change, from visible causes, which can alter the length of life. In the clause 'if you knew', al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan supply an implied answer: the people would hasten to repent.

Noah tells his Lord what he has endured from his people: he called them to the worship of God and to obedience, by night and by day, without pause, yet his calling only made them flee further. The commentators explain that "night and day" means a constant, uninterrupted invitation at every opportunity. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi agree that the core of the verse is their flight and persistence in refusal. They report that the people put their fingers in their ears and covered their faces with their garments so as not to hear or see the one who advised them, out of aversion to his message.

On the word "persisted" (asarru) there are several views. Al-Tabari and Ibn Zayd understand it as continuing in evil and disbelief, al-Hasan as committing sin deliberately, and al-Suddi as keeping silent about one's sins without seeking forgiveness. As for "arrogance," al-Dahhak takes it as disbelief and denial of Noah, while Ibn Abbas takes it as refusing to repent.

The commentators also note that Noah proceeded in stages: first in private, then openly, then combining the two. Al-Zamakhshari explains that "then" (thumma) signals the distance between these states, since open proclamation is harsher than discretion. Noah then urged them to seek forgiveness, promising worldly benefits in return: abundant rain, wealth, children and gardens with rivers. Several reports relate that al-Hasan al-Basri advised repentance to those who complained of drought or poverty, citing this passage, and Ibn Atiyya stresses that such repentance must be sincere in both words and deeds.

Opinions also differ on the phrase "you do not hope for dignity from God." Mujahid and Ibn Zayd read it as "you do not magnify God," Ibn Abbas as "you do not fear His consequence," and some as a rebuke for not expecting reward. Al-Razi draws from the verse a proof that events occur by God's decree, since the same call produces guidance in one listener and aversion in another.

Noah reports to his Lord the long, tireless effort he made with his people, calling them by night and by day. The commentators explain that his call only increased their flight, meaning that they turned further away from the truth and from obedience to God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read this as fleeing and turning away, while al-Mawardi gives two possible senses, fleeing from obedience or from accepting worship of God, and al-Sam'ani takes it as flight from faith. Al-Zamakhshari, followed by al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud, explains that the increase in flight is attributed to the call because it was its cause. The commentators agree that stopping their ears, covering their faces, persisting and being arrogant all show deep stubbornness. Ibn Atiyya notes that the word for persisting is mostly used of sins, and that these actions may be read literally or figuratively. The text then describes how Noah varied his preaching, first in private, then openly, then both together, which al-Zamakhshari reads as a gradual move from the gentlest to the firmest approach. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that seeking forgiveness brings rain and wealth, and Al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari cite a report of Umar praying for rain through seeking forgiveness alone. Ibn Atiyya holds that the forgiveness meant is sincere devotion, not the words alone.

Noah tells his Lord that he called his people night and day without pause, yet his call only made them flee further. Each time he invited them to faith, the way to the forgiveness of their sins, they stopped their ears with their fingers, covered their faces with their garments so as not to see or hear him, persisted in disbelief, and grew arrogant with a great arrogance. The commentators note that his preaching moved through stages: first in private, then in public, then combining the two. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take this as evidence of his earnest sincerity, while Abu Hayyan sees it as a progression of his outreach.

The commentators agree that persistence (al-israr) means holding firmly to wrongdoing. Ibn Zayd and Qatada take it as remaining in evil, al-Hasan as committing sin deliberately, and al-Suddi as failing to seek forgiveness after sinning. As for arrogance, al-Dahhak links it to disbelief and the denial of Noah, while Ibn 'Abbas links it to refusing to repent. Al-Raghib, cited by al-Alusi, defines persistence as entrenchment in sin and refusal to abandon it.

On the gesture itself, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take the stopping of ears and covering of faces literally, whereas Ibn Juzayy, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi read it as a vivid image of total aversion. Al-Qurtubi and al-Qasimi take the covering with garments as a figurative sign of hostility. The commentators leave these readings side by side without settling between them.

This passage of Surah Nuh recounts what Nuh, peace be upon him, said to his people after a long stay among them: he called them openly and loudly, then combined proclamation with private appeal, addressing groups at times and speaking to individuals alone at other times. The commentators agree that "jihaaran" means openly, without concealment, that "a'lantu" means calling out and raising the voice, and that "asrartu" refers to a private appeal between the prophet and the person addressed. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the word "thumma" marks a gradation in the stages of his preaching, public proclamation being harsher than private counsel, and that combining both was more forceful than using either alone.

Opinions differ on what the private appeal meant. Al-Tabari and Ibn Abbas, as reported by al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, explain that he spoke to each man in turn, privately between the two of them. Ibn Kathir presents it as a discreet appeal meant to be more effective. Al-Sam'ani and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that calling out and making oneself heard by a crowd amounts to the same thing, while the private element is speaking to one person alone.

The commentators agree on the substance of the call: seeking forgiveness from God, meaning repentance from disbelief and idolatry, which would bring abundant rain and prosperity. Several cite the example of Umar ibn al-Khattab, who asked for rain through istighfar alone, and of al-Hasan al-Basri, who advised seeking forgiveness during drought.

Noah tells his Lord what he has suffered from his people. He says he called them by night and by day, yet his calling only increased their flight, and whenever he invited them to faith so that they might be forgiven, they put their fingers in their ears, covered themselves with their garments, persisted and grew arrogant. The verse then describes how his method changed: he called them openly, then combined public proclamation with private address. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid explain the public call as shouting and the private one as speaking to each person separately. The commentators agree that this gradation shows his sincere advice and gentle approach, and that combining open and private appeals is stronger than either alone. Al-Zamakhshari reads the word 'then' as signalling the distance between these stages, openness being the stronger of the two. The following verses urge them to seek forgiveness, promising abundant rain, wealth and children. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report Umar's prayer for rain by seeking forgiveness, reciting this passage. Scholars differ on the meaning of 'you do not hope for dignity from Allah': Mujahid and Ikrima take it as not recognising His greatness, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr as not fearing His punishment or hoping for His reward, and al-Hasan as not knowing His right nor thanking Him. The commentators then turn to the stages of human creation, the seven heavens, the moon and the sun, and the earth spread out as a path for you to walk through wide roads.

Noah tells his Lord that he called his people by night and by day, openly and in private, and that his calling only increased their flight. In this verse he commands them to seek forgiveness from their Lord and repent of their polytheism and sins, for He is Oft-Forgiving to those who turn back to Him. The commentators agree that the istighfar here means repenting from disbelief and abandoning the worship of others, and that the command is an encouragement to faith. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir understand that the sending of abundant rain is the promised reward, with God also granting wealth, children, gardens and rivers. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that Noah began with rain because his people were suffering drought, while Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite the account of 'Umar, who went out to ask for rain, contented himself with seeking forgiveness and recited this verse, which they take as evidence that such istighfar brings rain. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya add that the forgiveness meant is not mere words but sincerity in speech and deeds. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes istighfar, which protects from past harm, from repentance, which also concerns the future. As for midrar, most read it as abundant, continuous rain, while al-Alusi allows that the word 'sky' may refer to the cloud or to the rain itself.

This verse tells of what Noah promised his people if they asked their Lord for forgiveness and turned to Him: God would send down the sky upon them in abundant, continuous rain. Most commentators understand 'the sky' here as the rain itself, though al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also mention the cloud, and Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi allow that the canopy of heaven or the cloud may be meant. All agree that 'midrar' means rain pouring down abundantly and without interruption. The commentators agree that seeking forgiveness and repentance is the cause of the rain and of other blessings. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy cite the report of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who went out to seek rain, only asked for forgiveness, and then recited this verse; Ibn Juzayy concludes from it that forgiveness brings down the rains. Ibn al-Qayyim draws from the verse a basis for regular seeking of forgiveness to obtain provision and relief, and Ibn Kathir recommends reciting this surah in the prayer for rain. Ibn Ashur explains that the worldly promise comes first because it is closer to people's hearts, while the reward of the hereafter is implied. Al-Razi observes that people are naturally drawn to immediate benefits, which is why God mentions the goods of this life. Several commentators note that Noah's people had suffered drought and barrenness for forty years, which made the promise of rain especially fitting. Concerning the meaning of 'istighfar,' Ibn Ashur and al-Alusi stress that repentance and seeking forgiveness are closely linked, and Ibn Kathir treats them as one act. The commentators report these views without choosing between them.

This verse reports Noah's words to his people: if you seek forgiveness from your Lord and turn back to Him, He will send down abundant, continuous rain upon you, increase your wealth and children, give you gardens and make rivers flow for you. Most commentators read the phrase 'What is the matter with you that you do not hope for dignity from Allah' as meaning that you do not magnify Allah as He deserves nor fear His power; this is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi. Qatada took it to mean you do not hope for a good outcome, Ibn Zayd that you do not render Him obedience, and al-Hasan that you do not acknowledge His rights or thank Him for His blessings. On the word 'rajaa', Abu Ubayda, Ibn Qutayba and al-Tabari gave it the sense of fear, citing a line of Abu Dhu'ayb, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understood it as hope that you would contemplate Allah's grandeur toward you, al-Razi rejecting the sense of fear as linguistically unsound. For 'He created you in stages', most cite the embryonic phases from drop to clot to lump of flesh until completion, while others understand the diversity of states, colours and characters. The commentators note that Noah addressed a people attached to worldly goods and so invited them through what they loved. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relate Umar's prayer for rain through seeking forgiveness alone, and Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan mention differences of reading and grammar in several words.

Noah complains to God about what he has endured from his people, then rebukes them: what is the matter with you that you do not hope for Allah any dignity (waqar)? In other words, why do you not revere God as He deserves, since He created you in stages, from a drop of semen to a clinging form and then a lump of flesh? The commentators agree on the general sense: waqar means greatness and the reverence due to God, and his listeners fall short of it. They differ on the word 'hope'. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Qutrub take it to mean fear or indifference, citing the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb, and al-Farra' explains that hope contains a trace of fear. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-'Aliya and 'Ata' say it means not hoping for reward nor fearing punishment. Qatada takes it as hoping for the good outcome of faith, Ibn Zayd as hoping to render obedience, and al-Hasan as recognising God's favours. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Juzayy read the phrase as an indirect call to faith. Al-Tabari prefers the sense of fearing God's greatness, since hope used with a negation implies fear. As for the 'stages', Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada understand them as the phases of the embryo's development, while others take them as the changing states of human life or the diversity of human types.

The commentators explain that God created human beings in successive stages, or states, one after another: a drop of fluid, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then bones clothed in flesh until the creation was complete. This is the explanation of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir. Some, such as Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy, extend the meaning to the differences among people in height, strength, health, wealth and character after birth. The verse belongs to Nuh's appeal to his people to believe in God alone: he rebukes them for failing to honour God while they can see the signs of His power in their own bodies. On the phrase 'ma lakum la tarjuna lillahi waqaran', opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir read it as 'you do not recognise God's greatness' or 'you do not honour Him as He deserves'. Al-Farra', Ibn Qutayba, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Tabari take the verb 'hope' to mean 'fear', so the sense is 'you do not fear God's majesty'. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya suggest hoping for God's reward or for the final outcome of faith. Al-Hasan understands it as failing to acknowledge God's rights and His favours. Al-Tabari prefers the sense of fear, while the other commentators do not settle the question. All agree that the verse calls for faith, gratitude and reverence towards God, and that reflection on the creation of man is evidence of His power.

Noah reminds his people of God's power in creating seven heavens layered one above another, placing the moon as a light within them and the sun as a lamp, and in creating them from the earth, returning them to it and bringing them out again. The commentators agree that the plain meaning is an argument from the greatness of creation: since God created all this, He alone deserves worship and reverence. On the word tibaqan, Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Kathir understand that each heaven covers the one below like domes, whereas al-Hasan says there are seven heavens above seven earths, with creation and command between each. As for the moon, al-Akhfash, al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that it is in the lowest heaven, and that the phrase 'in them' means that since it is in one of them it is in all of them. Ibn Abbas and Abdullah ibn Amr report that the faces of the sun and moon are turned toward the heavens and their backs toward the earth, while al-Suddi says the light is for the people of earth and Ata says for the people of heaven and earth alike. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud see these signs as proofs of the Creator's majesty. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan distinguish between light and lamp, holding that the sun's brightness is stronger than the moon's glow. On the stages of human creation, Ibn Abbas and Qatada explain them as the drop, the clinging clot and the lump of flesh. Ibn Kathir notes that this sura is recited in the prayer for rain, since seeking forgiveness brings rain and provision. The scholars agree that faith and monotheism are the path to good in this world and the next.

The commentators explain that this verse is part of Noah's address to his people, in which he urges them to reflect on the creation of the seven heavens as evidence of God's power and oneness. The plain meaning is that God placed the moon as a light within the heavens and made the sun a lamp by which the people of the earth see what they need to see. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi agree that the moon is in the nearest heaven, and that ascribing it to all the heavens is permitted in Arabic, just as one says "I visited the Banu Tamim" when one has only visited some of them.

Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar and Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As report that the faces of the sun and the moon are turned toward the heavens and their backs toward the earth, while other views reverse this. Al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur explain that light (nur) is weaker than brightness (diya'), which is why the sun is called a lamp and the moon a light, and they cite the verse He made the sun a brightness and the moon a light. Ibn Ashur adds that the image of a lamp brings the meaning closer to the listener and suits the rhyme of the passage. On the sun's exact place, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan note a disagreement between the fourth and fifth heavens, and Ibn Kathir reports the views of the astronomers on the planets without choosing between them.

The commentators draw no legal rulings from this passage. They read it mainly as a proof of divine power and an invitation to reflection.

This verse in Surah Nuh says that God brought humanity into being from the earth, and the commentators agree that the word 'make grow' is a metaphor for creation. Since Adam was made from the earth and human beings are nourished by its produce, the phrase is taken to mean that God created you from the earth and you grew as a plant grows. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that 'nabatan' is a noun used in place of the regular verbal noun, or an absolute object that stresses the verb. Al-Khalil and al-Zajjaj hold that the verb and noun must be understood together, as 'He made you grow, so you grew.' For the rest of the verse, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi understand 'He will return you into it' as burial after death, and 'bring you forth' as resurrection on the Day of Judgment. Ibn Kathir places the verse within Nuh's call to his people to worship God alone. Al-Razi observes that the choice of 'nabatan' over the verbal noun 'inbat' points to a visible growth that is easier to observe. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the verb 'make grow' is used for creation because human formation and plant growth both come from the earth. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Juzayy discuss the earth being spread like a carpet, and Ibn Juzayy rejects reading this as a proof that the earth is flat. The commentators therefore agree on the general meaning of creation, death and resurrection, and their differences concern the wording, and whether the verse refers to Adam or to all of humankind.

This passage of Surah Nuh says that God created human beings from the earth, will return them to it through death and burial, and will then bring them out of it on the Day of Resurrection, a certain bringing forth. The commentators agree that "He will return you into it" refers to death and burial, and "bring you forth" to the rising from the graves on the Day of Judgment. The emphatic infinitive "ikhrajan" is understood to stress the certainty of this event.

Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that "nabatan" means the creation of mankind from the dust of the earth, and that Adam was formed from the substance of the whole earth, as Ibn Jurayj reported. Ibn Bahr instead took it to mean that people grow in the earth, from youth to old age, and from short to tall. Al-Farra, al-Zajjaj and al-Khalil explain that "nabatan" is a noun used in place of the verbal noun, meaning that you were made to grow and you grew. Al-Zamakhshari reads the verb "anbata" as a metaphor for creation, which he finds more telling of the recent origin of humankind.

The commentators also agree that God spread the earth out like a carpet so that people could settle on it and travel its roads. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan note that some scholars drew from the word "bisatan" the conclusion that the earth is flat rather than spherical, a point Ibn Juzayy considered open to question, while others such as Ibn Ashur did not raise it. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur stress the link between the first creation and the resurrection: the One who can originate creation can bring it back.

The commentators explain that God made the earth spread out and smooth, a carpet on which people settle and move about as one moves on a rug, and that He made it so that you could travel along its wide and varied paths. Noah says this to remind his people of God's blessings. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree that "bisat" means spread out and levelled, and Ibn Kathir adds that the earth was made firm by the mountains. All take "subul fijaj" to mean varied or wide roads, with a fajj being a broad way, sometimes between two mountains according to al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan. The disagreement concerns what the word "bisat" tells us about the shape of the earth. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan judge its apparent sense to be a flat rather than spherical earth, Ibn 'Atiyya noting that some drew an argument from the sea surrounding the inhabited world, while al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur read it as an eloquent image of evenness and stability rather than a description of volume. Al-Alusi adds that belief in its shape is not a binding matter of religious law. Ibn Juzayy considers that deriving a flat, non-spherical earth from this word is open to question. All agree that the verse is framed as a blessing and as an argument for God's power.

This verse says that God made the earth spread out like a carpet, so that people could walk on it along wide and varied paths. It is part of Noah's speech to his people, in which he lists God's blessings and signs in the creation of the heavens and the earth. The commentators agree that "subul" means paths and that "fijaj" means wide roads: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi describe them as varied or broad routes, while al-Farra and Ibn al-Jawzi define a fajj as a wide road. Al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi add that a fajj may be the passage between two mountains.

On the word "bisat", al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy understand it as a flat, extended earth. Ibn Juzayy notes that some drew from this word the conclusion that the earth is not spherical, a view he considers open to question. Al-Alusi replies that the word does not settle the matter, that it is not an obligatory point of doctrine, and that the image is a comparison with the ease of the ground. Ibn Ashur clarifies that the comparison concerns the evenness of the surface rather than the overall shape.

Finally, the commentators connect this blessing to the other signs of creation that Noah mentions, so as to call people to worship the One God, as al-Jaza'iri notes.

This verse records Noah's complaint to his Lord: his people disobeyed him and followed their leaders, the wealthy notables whose wealth and children only increased their loss. The commentators explain that these riches, far from being a blessing, fed their pride and misguidance. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree that the followers were the common and weak people, and those they followed were the chiefs and the great. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan describe the people's great scheming: they plotted against Noah, incited others against him and turned them away from listening to him. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read the word kubbaran as an intensive form meaning very great, while Ibn Zayd takes it simply as great, and the readers differ on its vocalisation. The leaders told their followers not to abandon their gods, naming Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr. Al-Bukhari, cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, reports that these names first belonged to righteous men whose images were made, and that the images were later worshipped after knowledge faded. On the phrase 'they have led many astray', al-Tabari and most commentators attribute it to the chiefs, whereas Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari, as a second reading, apply it to the idols. As for the prayer that the wrongdoers receive only further misguidance, al-Zamakhshari understands it as divine abandonment and the withholding of favours, Ibn Bahr as punishment, and others as ruin and loss.

Nuh tells his Lord that his people disobeyed him, and that the followers, the lowly, followed leaders whose wealth and children only increased their loss. As for the phrase "and they schemed a tremendous scheme", the commentators agree that it is a very great and severe plot, linked grammatically to the relative clause about the one whom wealth did not enrich, with the chiefs as its authors. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid explain that "kubbaran" means great and immense, and that the intensive form is stronger than the plain one, as in similar Arabic pairs. They differ on what the scheme consisted of. Ibn Abbas takes it as monstrous speech, al-Dahhak as slander against God and rejection of His messengers, and others as inciting the common folk to kill Nuh. Al-Kalbi relates it to what they attributed to God of companions and offspring, while Muqatil relates it to the chiefs' words to their followers: do not abandon your gods, Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq, or Nasr. Most exegetes report that these names were once righteous men whose images were made and later worshipped, and that the idols then passed to Arab tribes, such as Wadd among the Kalb and Nasr among Himyar. Readers differ on the vowel of Wadd and on whether Yaghuth and Ya'uq take tanwin, a reading Ibn Atiyya considers a mistake.

This passage from Surat Nuh records the words of the notables of Noah's people to their followers: do not abandon your gods, nor Wadd, nor Suwa', nor Yaghuth, nor Ya'uq, nor Nasr. The commentators understand these as the names of idols that this people worshipped, and that their leaders urged their followers to keep to them. They agree that these idols were later worshipped by the Arabs: Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Kathir and others report that Wadd belonged to the Kalb at Dawmat al-Jandal, Suwa' to the Hudhayl, Yaghuth to Murad and then the Banu Ghutayf, Ya'uq to Hamdan and Nasr to the Himyar. Most also relate a well-known account in which these were righteous men whose followers made images of them to remember them, and Satan later persuaded their descendants to worship those images after a long time. Al-Baghawi and al-Tha'labi mention that the names may have belonged to sons of Adam, while al-Wahidi and al-Waqidi describe different forms for each idol, and Ibn 'Ashur holds that the names survived among the believers saved with Noah before the Arabs took them up.

On recitation, the readers differ over the vowel of the waw in 'wuddan': Nafi' reads it with a damma, the others with a fatha, and the commentators regard both as valid. Al-A'mash and Ashhab read 'Yaghuthan wa Ya'uqan' with tanwin; Ibn 'Atiyya calls this an error, while Abu Hayyan explains it as a dialectal usage.

On the phrase 'and they have led many astray', al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir apply it to the idols that misled many people, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur take it to mean the great men of the nation who misled their followers. On 'and do not increase the wrongdoers except in error', al-Tabari understands a sealing of the heart, al-Zamakhshari a withdrawal of divine help, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi a prayer by Noah after he despaired of their faith, and Ibn Juzayy a curse upon them.

This verse reports Noah's prayer against his people after he despaired of their faith: they have led many astray, and he asks God to increase the wrongdoers only in error. Commentators differ on who the subject of "they have led astray" is. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy take it to be the leaders and notables who drew their followers into idolatry, while Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and others take it to be the idols themselves, which are spoken of with the pronoun for rational beings, as in Abraham's words "they have led many people astray." As for the error whose increase is requested, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya understand it as God withdrawing His grace and abandoning them, al-Razi sees a reference to their deceitful scheming, and al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir understand it as punishment or ruin, citing the verse "the criminals are in error and blaze." Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn 'Ashur reject a purely doctrinal sense, since it would clash with Noah's call to seek forgiveness. All agree on the identity of the idols. According to Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Kathir, Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr were righteous men of Noah's time whose images were made after their death and later worshipped; the idols then passed to Arab tribes: Kalb at Dawmat al-Jandal, Hudhayl, Murad, Hamdan and Himyar. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Qayyim also record the view that the statues were first made as reminders of the righteous, and Ibn al-Qayyim draws from this a warning against the veneration of tombs.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the fate of Noah's people after their prophet had despaired of their faith: they were drowned by the flood because of their sins, then made to enter the Fire, and they found no helpers besides God to save them from punishment. They agree that the drowning took place in this world by the flood, and that the sins meant include polytheism, rejecting the messenger, harming him, and other wrongdoing. The past tense used for entering the Fire is, in their view, a way of affirming that it is certain to occur. They differ on when this entry happened. Ibn Zayd, Muqatil, al-Kalbi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as taking place in the Hereafter, while al-Dahhak holds that they were punished in this world, drowning on one side and burning on the other. Al-Tabari, al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud see it rather as the punishment of the grave or the intermediate state, the particle fa indicating that it followed immediately. On recitation, Abu 'Amr reads khataya-hum, while the majority reads khati'atihim. Al-Zamakhshari notes that placing the prepositional phrase before the verb emphasises that their sins were the cause of the drowning. The verse belongs to Noah's supplication against the disbelievers that follows it. The commentators draw the lesson that polytheism and sin lead to ruin, and that the deities worshipped besides God can help no one on the day of punishment.

Noah, having despaired of his people's faith, prays to his Lord: do not leave upon the earth any disbeliever who roams it. The commentators explain that the word dayyar is a general negative term meaning any single person, derived from the root of moving about or of the dwelling, as al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba state. They agree that this people's destruction came because of its sins: they were drowned and then sent into the fire, and they found no helpers besides God. To justify his prayer, Noah relies on the revelation that only those who already believed would believe, and on his long experience with them, which made him fear that they would mislead his servants and beget only wicked disbelievers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report other accounts, such as Noah's anger after a man struck his son, or the view that the prayer concerned the dead. On the question of barrenness, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd say God made their wombs barren forty or seventy years before the punishment, while al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliya hold that the children perished without punishment. Noah then asks forgiveness for himself, his parents and the believers. The commentators differ on the meaning of his 'house': a mosque according to Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak, his dwelling, his ark, or his religion according to others.

The commentators place this verse within Noah's invocation against his people, made after he despaired of their faith. The meaning is that Noah feared that if his people were left alive they would lead his believers astray and would bear children destined for disbelief and wickedness. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and Muqatil report that a man would bring his son to Noah and warn him against him, so that the elder died while the younger grew up with that same suspicion. As for the phrase 'they will beget none but wicked disbelievers', most scholars read it as describing what they will become, that is, those who will be wicked and disbelieving. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi hold that Noah knew this through revelation and through his long experience with them. The reports differ on the cause of the supplication. Qatada links it to the revelation that none will believe except those who already have, while others recount the incident of the child who struck Noah on the head. Muhammad ibn Ka'b, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd say that God caused their wombs to be barren forty or seventy years before the punishment. Al-Hasan and Abu al-Aliya maintain that God destroyed the children without punishment, whereas Qatada says there were no children present at the time of the punishment. Ibn al-Qayyim argues that the verse does not conflict with the natural purity of the newborn, since 'wicked' and 'disbelieving' describe future states. All agree that Noah then prayed for himself, his parents and the believers, though they differ on the 'house': Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes take it as the mosque, while others take it as his home, his ark or his religion.

After despairing of his people's faith, Noah asks his Lord to forgive him, his parents, whoever enters his house as a believer, all believing men and women, and to increase the wrongdoers only in ruin. The commentators agree that the prayer for believers is general, and that tabar means destruction or loss. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report, following Qatada, that Noah prayed for their destruction only after being told that none of his people would believe except those who already had, while al-Hasan gives another cause: a man carried his small son on his shoulders and warned him against Noah, who was then struck on the head. On the meaning of the house, Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi take it as the mosque, while others take it as the dwelling, the ark, or the religion and law. On the parents, al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir state they were believers, al-Tabari names them Lamak and Shamkha, others name Adam and Eve, and Ibn Abbas holds that no ancestor of Noah from Adam onward was an unbeliever. As for the children drowned with their people, al-Hasan says God destroyed them without punishment, others say God rendered the women barren before the flood, and Ibn Juzayy affirms that praying for all believers is permissible.
